Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion. It preferentially adsorbs at the protrusion to inhibit the copper deposition rate because of the selective adsorption of the quaternary ammonium cation [18]. Therefore, a proper addition of JGB results in a copper deposit with a mirror-like surface. It is an effective reagent for carrying out a void-free filling in dual damascene metallization [4,5,7,8,10]. With regard to the electrochemical and adsorptive behaviors of JGB on the copper electrodeposition, Li et al. [18] and Bozzini et al. [19] presented detailed results using various instruments to identify the molecular structures of adsorbed JGB and the byproduct thereof. In addition, JGB can interact with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to form a composite suppressor whose adsorptive behavior is strongly convection dependent [16,17]. Hence, the addition of JGB can significantly enhance the filling performance of a plating formula because the forced convection acting on the board surface is always stronger than that at the bottom of the microvia during electroplating [20,21]. The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23].

In this study, additive Sodium 3-(benzothiazole-2-ylthio)-1-pro panesulfonate (ZPS) has been systematically investigated for copper foil electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectra indicate that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM shows that the 3D diffusion controlled instantaneous nucleation and growth model is not changed but the active sites are increased by ZPS. Theoretical analysis suggests that ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and catch free $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ by -SO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> to accelerate the electro-reduction coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> through “bridging effect”. Adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed. Molecular dynamics simulation and in situ infrared spectroscopy verify the improved adsorption property of ZPS with increased cathodic polarization. A Turing oscillation growth model, validated by finite-element simulation and AFM, reveals that ZPS accumulates in valleys to locally accelerate growth, improving flatness via cyclic peakvalley transfer, but the smoothing effect is ultimately constrained by this oscillation. Structural characterization demonstrates that ZPS selectively promotes the Cu (220) crystal orientation and suppresses the (200) plane, while HRTEM directly visualizes twin boundaries, with lattice fringes showing a shift from (111) to (220) in twin-vicinity regions upon ZPS addition. EBSD confirms grain refinement (mean grain size reduced from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and a marked increase in twinboundary density, which together enhance mechanical performance through Hall-Petch strengthening and dislocation obstruction. Regarding copper foil performance, surface morphology is noticeably improved, while the optimal mechanical properties are achieved at 30 mg/L ZPS, yielding a tensile strength of 331 MPa and elongation of 3.78 %, attributed to grain refinement and twin-boundary strengthening. Finite-element simulation of skin effect demonstrates that the reduced roughness significantly lowers signal loss. Collectively, this work not only establishes ZPS as an effective single additive for industrial copper foil production but also advances the fundamental understanding of additive-induced structure-property relationships, offering a solid foundation for future additive design and process optimization.

Metal cobalt interconnect layer is mainly prepared by electrodeposition technology. In the process of metal cobalt electrodeposition, additives are key components that can adjust the cobalt deposition rate in via and trench, improve the uniformity of the deposited cobalt film, and thus improve chip performance [6–9]. However, due to the confidentiality of the technology, there are relatively few related studies and reports, but this does not affect its importance and application prospects. Li et al. [10] introduced that dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride could refine cobalt grains and achieve microvia superconformal filling. Huang et al. [11,12] showed that dimethylglyoxime had a strong suppression effect and made cobalt a three-dimensional nucleation. Wu et al. [13] discovered that Akyne-PEG4-amine could be used as an inhibitor to achieve nanometer scale superfilling of cobalt electrode position. Kiruba et al. [14] presented that butynediol (BD) would change the interfacial pH to regulate and control the formation of cobalt. It is worth noting that BD as a typical type-II brightener has attracted much attention among the many cobalt additives. Jeyabharathi et al. [15] deemed that BD would cause electrochemical oscillation due to the hydrogenation of BD during cobalt electrodeposition. Pan et al. [16] showed that BD and saccharin together could decrease the microhard ness of cobalt deposits as a result of increased grain size. Although it is well known that BD can be used as an additive, the effect of its molecular structure on the interface of cobalt electrodeposition has not been elucidated at a molecular level. Therefore, it is necessary to carry out relevant research. This study demonstrates the adsorption state of BD on cobalt surface and the effects of adsorption on crystal growth and orientation. This enriches the understanding of the role of additives in the cobalt electrodeposition process, revealing that BD achieves uniformity and compact film morphology through interactions with the cobalt surface, which is conducive to promote the development of high-performance chip interconnection technology.

In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.

Although NBT and PEG exhibit electrochemical behaviors that facilitate the superfilling of microvias, the achievement of efficient microvia superfilling electroplating often necessitates the synergistic effect of SPS. Specifically, SPS focuses on accelerating copper deposition at the bottom of the microvias, while PEG–NBT is responsible for suppressing copper deposition in the microvias’ entrance region. To fully predict a leveler’s performance, one must assess not only its electronic active sites but also its interactions with other species and their corresponding adsorption sites. Accordingly, DFT calculations were carried out to investigate NBT’s interactions with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ions and with the suppressor PEG. Atom in Molecules (AIM) and interaction region indicator (IRI) calculations were carried out for the ${ \mathrm { N B T } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ complex, while the NBT–PEG interaction was analyzed with the independent-gradient model based on Hirshfeld parti tion (IGMH), as shown in Figure 7. As shown in Figure $^ { 7 } \mathbf { a } ,$ the shortest contact between $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ and NBT is the Cu–N bond to the tetrazolium nitrogen (1.994 Å). The Cu–O distance to the methoxy group is longer (2.177 $\mathring \mathrm { A } )$ , indicating that the Cu–N interaction is stronger than the Cu–O one. To evaluate the bond nature, we calculated the bond-critical-point (BCP) parameters (Table 1). For both Cu–N and Cu–O bonds, the electron density at the BCP (ρ ) is below 0.10 a.u. and the Laplacian of electron density $( \nabla ^ { 2 } \rho _ { \mathrm { B C P } } )$ value is positive, showing that the two bonds for Cu–N and Cu–O are ionic bonds [47,48]. However, only the Cu–N bond has negative energy density $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { B C P } } \right)$ and negative potential energy density (Vr ), which confirms that the Cu–N bond is the stronger bond [49]. IRI analysis (Figure 7b) reveals blue isosurfaces between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the tetrazolium nitrogen, as well as between ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ and the methoxy oxygen, indicating strong Cu–N and Cu–O interactions. The two-dimensional IRI map (Figure 7c) further supports these observations, confirming robust coordination between NBT and $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ ions. These findings indicate that NBT coordi nates predominantly with ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ via the nitrogen atom of the tetrazolium ring, forming a strong ionic bond that retards ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ reduction. This selective coordination promotes NBT adsorption at Cu-rich sites—such as microvia mouths or cathode protrusions—thereby efficiently inhibiting local deposition.

This work investigated the influence of Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) as a single additive on performance of copper foil. Electrochemical analysis indicates that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu<sup>2+</sup> to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> . Furthermore, a Turing oscillation growth model, supported by finite element simulations and AFM analysis, is proposed to describe the morphological evolution, wherein ZPS preferentially accumulates at valley regions, improving surface flatness through cyclic peak-valley transfer, though with inherently limited ultimate smoothing. Structurally, XRD shows ZPS promotes Cu (220) orientation, while HRTEM confirms the presence of twin boundaries, and lattice fringe measurements reveal a transition from (111)-dominated to (220)-dominated regions upon ZPS addition. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. In terms of performance, ZPS improves surface morphology and reduces roughness. Mechanical properties are optimized at 30 mg/L ZPS, with tensile strength reaching 331 MPa and elongation 3.78 %. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

text: It is significantly important to develop novel suppressor to achieve cobalt superconformal filling. Linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and impedance spectra (EIS) were coupled together to study the effect of novel dye suppressor nitrotetrazolium blue chloride (NBT) on cobalt electrodeposition. The adsorption behavior of NBT on cobalt substrate was investigated by applying density functional theory (DFT) calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra, while the interaction between NBT and cobalt ions $( \mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + } )$ is analyzed based on topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis. Synergistic suppressing mechanism, namely adsorption effect and coordination effect, was proposed to explain the suppressing effect of NBT during cobalt electrodeposition. The cobalt surface morphology analysis under the influence of NBT demonstrates that NBT is of grain refinement, while XRD analysis indicates that the formation of Co hcp (100) is formed preferentially. The superconformal filling of cobalt is achieved in microvias with different diameters. The cobalt layer is of excellent quality due to low surface deposit thickness (SDT). The SDT values are 15.9 μm, 8.8 μm and 4.9 μm for 150 m, 100 m and 50 m.

MPS and PVP as additives exhibit the function of acceleration and inhibition during cobalt electrodeposition, respectively. They undergo competitive adsorption behavior in cobalt electrodeposition and some adsorption sites of MPS are replaced by PVP. The adsorption site was calculated by quantum chemical calculations. The amide groups of PVP and thiol groups of MPS are probably the adsorption sites in cobalt electrodeposition. Besides, the amide groups of PVP mainly contribute to the HOMO orbital as a probable main electrophilic attack region. The cobalt pillars with diferent diameters are successfully fabricated with the use of competitive adsorption between MPS and PVP. In this way, the additives of cobalt electrodeposition can efectively control the process of electrodeposition and a uniform cobalt deposition could be obtained. Cobalt electrodeposition has great potential in system-in-package, and this work facilitates the theoretical research and application of cobalt pillar in electronic interconnection. Synthesis of additives and more theoretical studies focusing on the working mechanism of the additives in cobalt electrodeposition are expected in the future.

In this work, electrochemical analysis methods, including cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectra and EQCM were used to study the suppressing effect of NBT on cobalt electrodeposition. Besides, in situ Raman spectra was used to analyze the suppressing mechanism and NBT can absorb on cobalt surface to suppress the cobalt electrodeposition. EQCM-derived coulomb-voltage curves indicates that high pH is beneficial for the cobalt electrodeposition. Finite element method was accepted to simulate the influence of NBT concentration on convection. Besides, NBT can benefit the HER, which can effectively intensify the local mass transfer during electrodeposition. The intensified local mass transfer can further supply suppressor NBT to cathode surface so as keep the deposition in plane suppressed. Suppressingaccelerating effect is proposed to illustrate the effect of NBT. On one hand, NBT can adsorb on cathode surface to suppress cobalt deposition. On the other hand, NBT can boost the HER and the intensified gas releasing process in turn accelerate the mass transfer of NBT to strengthen the suppressing effect of NBT on cobalt electrodeposition.

The deposit leveller takes an important role in plating-related processes such as copper damascene interconnection,<sup>1–3</sup> copper pillar bumps,<sup>4,5</sup> and microvias.<sup>6,7</sup> Janus Green B (JGB) is the commonly used leveller which has been studied extensively. Kelly et $a I . ^ { 1 }$ and Cao et $a / . ^ { 8 }$ firstly proposed a four-component additive containing JGB to achieve the levelling efect and suggested a competitive adsorption relationship between these additives. Dow et al.<sup>9–11</sup> found that the inhibiting efect of JGB was enhanced in the presence of convection and proposed the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) theory, suggesting that the CDA behaviour of the additive was a crucial factor to achieve bottom-up filling. Li et $a I . ^ { 1 2 }$ determined the structure of the reduction product of JGB by mass spectrometry (MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and proposed that the reduction product of JGB is the true leveller in the copper filling process. Mao et al.<sup>13</sup> provided molecular spectroscopic evidence on the reductive decomposition of the JGB azo group by in-situ attenuated total reflection-surface enhanced infrared spectroscopy. Hai et al.<sup>14</sup> further stated that the consumption of JGB should also include the reduction of heterocycles. In the present authors’ previous work, JGB-induced convection-dependence has been observed,<sup>15</sup> but molecular-level understanding of its genesis is still absent.

The suppressing effect of dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT) on cobalt electrodeposition is investigated by LSV and EIS. Building on this insight, numerous researchers have designed levelers that incorporate either the azo or quaternary-ammonium group. Wang et al. employed gentian violet, which contains a positively charged quaternary-ammonium group, as a leveler for through-hole electrodeposition and demonstrated that this leveler exhibited plating performance as excellent as that of JGB [16]. However, other researchers introduced quaternary-ammonium groups with varying chain lengths onto the quinacridone skeleton to develop a novel leveler [17], and the novel leveler exhibited superior plating performance compared to JGB. Taken together, these studies further confirm that the positively charged quaternary-ammonium group constitutes the key active functional moiety of leveler molecules.

Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) is studied in this paper as an inhibitor of cobalt electrodeposition. The suppres sion effect of PVP was analyzed through electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and galvanostatic measurements (GM) tests. It is indicated that PVP effectively suppresses the electrodeposition of cobalt and chloride ion accelerates this suppression. Further experiments verify that PVP inhibits the deposition of cobalt through the adsorption on the electrode surface. Quantum chemical calculations were employed to calculate the molecular orbitals of PVP and the electrostatic potential (ESP) energy of the involved molecules. High aspect ratio trench filling on silicon wafer was achieved with the addition of PVP, which confirms that PVP is an applicable inhibitor for the practical electrodeposition of cobalt filling. The mechanism of cobalt trench filling was proposed to explain the role of PVP in the electroplating filling. Besides, crystalline and morphological characterizations reveal that PVP is able to inhibit the specific crystal growth of cobalt. especially the growth of 220 crystal plane. affect the crystal morphology of cobalt and improve surface compactness.

The manufacture process of cobalt interconnects is similar to that of copper interconnects and is compatible with existing electrodeposition processes for copper damascene interconnects. The electrodeposition process for cobalt interconnection is an advanced interconnect technology for integrated circuits that utilizes a wet electrochemical deposition method to bottom-up fill the interconnect structures of semiconductor chips with cobalt metal. Electrodeposition has the advantages of simple operation, easy control of process parameters, and low cost and is considered to be the main technology for cobalt filling at present.<sup>16−18</sup> In recent years, the process of copper electrodeposition has been thoroughly studied, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the bottom-up electro deposition (superfilling) mechanism, which is also applied to cobalt electrodeposition to achieve defect-free interconnect structures.<sup>19,20</sup>

Abstract: Copper interconnect technology faces limitations due to the electron’s mean free path and electromigration, driving the adoption of cobalt alternatives. This study proposes a novel mechanism to achieve superfilling by tuning the adsorption energy of additive molecules on cobalt surfaces. The adsorption energies of additives are tailored by changing molecular structures with different functional groups. Computational results reveal that carbon–carbon triple bonds critically strengthen adsorption, while ether bonds further enhance binding on distinct cobalt crystallographic planes. Specifically, 1,4-bis(2- hydroxyethoxy)-2-butyne (BEO) containing both triple bonds and ether groups exhibits the highest adsorption energy (−22.62 eV). Replacing ether with hydroxyl groups in 2- butyne-1,4-diol (BOZ) reduces the adsorption energy to −10.39 eV, while eliminating triple bonds in 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDE) further decreases it to −8.43 eV. Experimental studies demonstrate that BOZ and BEO preferentially adsorb on the (101) and (110) planes of hexagonal close-packed cobalt (HCP-Co) due to their differential adsorption energies. This selective suppression promotes preferential growth along the densely packed (002) orientation. This leads to a trench-filling process dominated by the most densely packed plane, resulting in better electrical performance. Superfilling is achieved when molecular adsorption energies are in the range of 5–8 eV. The work establishes a functional group design strategy to regulate additive adsorption, enabling crystallographic control for advanced cobalt electrodeposition processes.

Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling.
